data.name: Choice of Rebels: Uprising
data.detailed_description:
Lead the revolt against a bloodthirsty empire! You grew up under the iron fist of the Hegemony. Now is your chance to end their blood-fueled magic, as you forge a ragtag outlaw band into a rebel army.

Choice of Rebels: Uprising is a 637,000 word interactive fantasy novel by Joel Havenstone, where your choices control the story. It's entirely text-based—without graphics or sound effects—and fueled by the vast, unstoppable power of your imagination.

As an outlaw rebel in the greenwood wilderness, you must steal to survive your first brutal winter, or watch your people starve if you can't feed them. Win yeomen, helots, merchants, priests, and aristocrats over to the rebel cause...or turn them into your worst enemies. Will you defeat the army of the Hegemony’s Archon and the elite force of evil blood mages sent to destroy you, or will a personal betrayal put an end to your rebellion when it’s just barely begun?

  • Play as male or female, gay, straight, or ace
  • Fight as a renegade aristocrat or defiant slave
  • Lead your outlaw band as a self-taught mage, a general, or a mystic priest
  • Reform the empire’s religion or start your own
  • Master the arcane magic of Theurgy and demolish the blood harvesters of the Hegemony
  • Find romance amongst your fellow young rebels
  • Root out spies, betrayers, and fend off a mutiny
  • Survive attacks from assassins, mages, and the mutant Plektoi hounds

Will you gain a reputation as a compassionate idealist or ruthless insurgent? Can your rebels survive the winter and a vengeful army?

How much will you sacrifice to rebel, and save your homeland from an oppressive empire?

reviews.review:
[h1]CHOICE OF MULES[/h1]

Choice of Rebels: Uprising is an Interactive Fiction game set in a mature, low-fantasy world where your choices truly matter.
I was able to finish it in around 7 hours, but if you want to explore different routes, you can easily spend 15 hours or more. 
Honestly, I'm a little bit torn about Uprising. On one hand, it features a compelling story with various meaningful choices, but on the other hand, it can be very stats-heavy and repetitive. While this wasn't a major issue for me, fans of "traditional" interactive fiction may find Uprising a bit too gamey.
Overall, I found the experience entertaining and definitely [b]can recommend it[/b]. It’s certainly not for everyone, but if you're fine with resource management, you'll probably like it.

[b]World[/b]
There's a lot of worldbuilding throughout the game. At first, this can be slightly overwhelming due to the constant introduction of new names and titles, but it doesn't take long to get used to it. One small nitpick of mine: some names try a bit too hard to sound "fantasy" for no reason. Starting a name with the letter X doesn't automatically make it more unique.
Initially, you only learn what you absolutely need to know - how things operate, who the bad guy is, and who is struggling and why. However, the longer you play, the more information you discover about the world. Fortunately, the lore is spread out well enough that you never have to deal with overwhelming, bloated info-dumps.

[b]Story[/b]
The main story is fairly simple but well-written. You start the game as either a helot (slave) or an aristocrat, and you very quickly get entangled in a rebel plot to overthrow a bloodthirsty empire. Thanks to your abilities - and the fact that you're the main character, of course - you rapidly become one of the leaders of the rebellion. From there, you must find a way to secure a victory, or at the very least, survive. What happens next depends entirely on your choices.
There is also a side plot involving a traitor hidden within your band, but it often feels like the game expects you to ignore it. Every now and then, you're told that something suspicious has occurred, and you even get the option to execute an accused member, but it never escalates into anything major. Ultimately, it feels like setup for a larger narrative in a second or third Choice of Rebels title, but for now, only the first game has been released on Steam.

[b]Characters[/b]
I didn't find most of the characters very interesting. With the exception of Breden - where you're never 100% sure whether they are a traitor or not - they didn't offer anything unique to the story. Perhaps I would feel differently if we spent more meaningful time with them, but it often felt like they were just there as a background element to move the plot forward.
Obviously, I'm not saying they are all bad. Most of them, like Zvad or Elery, have their moments, but in my opinion, it's simply not enough. The game would heavily benefit from cutting down on some of the micromanagement and instead giving players more opportunities to bond with their companions. Hell, you could probably even combine the two mechanics in some way.
If you're interested in romance, Breden is the only sensible option. They are the only character with enough buildup to make the relationship feel earned.

[b]Choices & Stats[/b]
Choice of Rebels is a very stat-heavy game, and a single poor decision can completely make or break your playthrough. Is this a bad thing? It depends on what you enjoy. Personally, it didn't bother me too much, but there were definitely moments (trying to survive the winter) where the experience became frustratingly repetitive. Additionally, it was sometimes difficult to gauge what the author considered the optimal choice. For instance, how am I supposed to know exactly how much money will satisfy the farmers without looking up a guide? This wouldn't be such a major issue with a standard save system, but it is what it is.  
There is an option to delegate camp management to one of your companions, but if you want to achieve the best possible run, you have to micromanage everything yourself. It's also important to remember that selecting your character's starting strengths at the beginning of the game is highly impactful, as it drastically alters the difficulty of certain segments. 
The choices themselves are excellent - they are plentiful and often carry visible consequences. Granted, some outcomes are predictable (not enough food means people die), but others are much harder to foresee. Missed out on a raid because you lacked the resources? Well, you won't get that new companion. 
Choice of Rebels is definitely not a game where you'll see everything in a single playthrough. Since various outcomes are locked behind specific paths, you are heavily incentivized to try another run with different skills and choices.

[b]Audio & Visuals[/b]
This game is purely text-based, so there’s not much to comment on in terms of audio or visuals. Still, I’ll leave my usual note for interactive fiction: even basic visuals and audio could make these games more accessible and appealing to a wider audience, similar to what Roadwarden or Wayfarer have done.

[b]Technicalities[/b]
The lack of a save system - or at least a "back to the previous page" button - is just incredibly frustrating. I can’t stress enough how much I dislike it when interactive fiction games do this. It’s all too easy to misclick on a choice you didn’t intend, especially in longer games, so give players a way to fix it.
I didn't notice any bugs, typos, or other issues.
